content: Ranitidine, also known by its International Nonproprietary Name (INN), is a histamine H2-receptor antagonist that works by inhibiting the production of stomach acid. It is frequently prescribed for the treatment of peptic ulcer disease (PUD) and gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD). The drug is available over the counter under brand names such as Zinetac and Zantac, marketed by GlaxoSmithKline and other pharmaceutical companies under various trade names. Certain formulations of ranitidine are sold over the counter (OTC) in different countries. In the United States, 75 mg and 150 mg tablets are available without a prescription. In Australia, packs containing 7 or 14 doses of the 150 mg tablet can be purchased in supermarkets, while smaller packs of 150 mg and 300 mg tablets are classified as Schedule 2 Pharmacy Medicines. Larger doses and pack sizes still require a prescription. Outside the United States, ranitidine is sometimes combined with bismuth, which has mild antibiotic properties, in the form of ranitidine bismuth citrate (marketed as Tritec) to treat infections caused by Helicobacter pylori. This combination is often administered alongside clarithromycin, an antibiotic. Ranitidine was developed by Glaxo (now GlaxoSmithKline) as part of an effort to replicate the success of cimetidine, the first histamine H2-receptor antagonist, which was developed by Smith, Kline & French (also now GlaxoSmithKline). The creation of ranitidine was the result of a rational drug design process that utilized a refined model of the histamine H2-receptor and quantitative structure-activity relationships (QSAR). Glaxo improved upon the existing model by replacing the imidazole ring of cimetidine with a furan ring containing a nitrogen-based substituent, leading to the development of ranitidine. This modification resulted in a drug with fewer adverse reactions, a longer duration of action, and ten times the potency of cimetidine. Ranitidine has only 10% of the affinity for cytochrome P450 enzymes compared to cimetidine, which reduces the likelihood of drug-drug interactions and side effects. However, other H2-receptor antagonists, such as famotidine and nizatidine, have no significant interactions with the cytochrome P450 system. Ranitidine was first introduced in 1981 and became the world’s best-selling prescription drug by 1988. Over time, it has been largely replaced by more effective proton pump inhibitors (PPIs), such as omeprazole, which became the top-selling drug for many years.
